practice_questions.text: Name the bone that sits in front of the knee joint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: patella / kneecap.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'blood cell production' as a function of the skeleton.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that red bone marrow produces blood cells; 1 mark for specifying red blood cells (which carry oxygen to working muscles during exercise) or white blood cells / platelets.

practice_questions.text: Describe how two of the six functions of the skeleton help a rugby player during a match.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming a valid function (e.g. protection); 1 mark for explaining that function physiologically (e.g. the ribs and sternum form a cage that shields the heart and lungs from impact forces during a tackle); 1 mark for a second distinct function applied to rugby (e.g. movement — the femur and tibia act as levers at the hip and knee, producing the explosive leg drive of a sprint). Accept any two of: support, posture, protection, movement, blood cell production, storage of minerals, each with a relevant rugby application.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the skeleton provides the function of posture during physical activity, and why this is different from the function of support.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining posture: the vertebral column and pelvis keep the body in correct mechanical alignment during movement; 1 mark for applying posture to sport (e.g. a rower must maintain spinal alignment throughout the drive to transfer force efficiently and avoid injury); 1 mark for explaining support: the skeleton bears the weight of the body against gravity so the body does not collapse; 1 mark for clearly distinguishing between them (support is about resisting gravity/bearing load; posture is about maintaining the correct shape and alignment for efficient and safe movement).

practice_questions.text: State two bones of the hand or foot that are named in the specification, and state where each is located in the body.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two hand or foot bones with a correct location: carpals (wrist / wrist bones), metacarpals (palm of the hand), phalanges (fingers / toes — accept either location), tarsals (ankle / heel bones), metatarsals (arch of the foot / foot bones between ankle and toes). Two marks awarded for two different bones each with a correct location.

practice_questions.text: A county-level hockey player relies on her skeleton for a range of functions during a match. Analyse how two functions of the skeleton contribute to her performance during the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two functions clearly identified and developed with accurate physiological explanation, each applied specifically to hockey performance. The candidate links structure to function (e.g. how the femur acts as a lever at the hip during a reverse hit; how red blood cells produced in bone marrow carry oxygen to support sustained aerobic play) and demonstrates understanding of how skeletal function supports overall performance throughout.

Secure: Two functions identified with mostly accurate explanation and applied to a general sporting context. Some links between structure and performance may be undeveloped.

Developing: One or two functions mentioned with limited development. Application to sport is vague or missing from one function.

Emerging: Basic naming of functions with little or no explanation or sporting application.

Acceptable content: movement (long bones as levers; femur pivots at the hip to produce the sweeping action of a reverse hit); protection (ribcage protects heart and lungs from stick or ball impact); posture (vertebral column maintains alignment when the player bends to receive a low ball); mineral storage (calcium stored in the skeleton maintains bone density under the repeated loading of running); blood cell production (red blood cells produced in bone marrow carry oxygen to working muscles during aerobic play).

practice_questions.text: Identify one organisation that collects data on current participation trends in physical activity and sport in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: Sport England (1); National Governing Body / NGB (1); Department for Culture, Media and Sport / DCMS (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'engagement patterns' in the context of physical activity and sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition identifying participation rates or who takes part in physical activity; 1 mark for linking this to different social groups or identifying inequalities in access. Example full-mark answer: 'Engagement patterns are the rates and patterns of participation in physical activity across different social groups in society, used to identify inequalities in access and involvement.'

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the percentage of people participating in at least 150 minutes of physical activity per week across four social groups in a local authority survey.

Social group | Participation rate
Men aged 18-30 | 61%
Women aged 18-30 | 43%
Adults with a disability | 28%
Adults aged 60+ | 35%

Using the data in Table 1, calculate the difference in participation between men aged 18-30 and adults with a disability. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working (61% - 28%); 1 mark for the correct answer (33); 1 mark for including the correct unit (percentage points or %). Full-mark answer: '61% - 28% = 33 percentage points. Men aged 18-30 participate at a rate 33 percentage points higher than adults with a disability.'

practice_questions.text: Using Table 1 above, interpret what the data shows about participation patterns across the four groups. Suggest one reason for the lowest participation rate shown.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the lowest participation group (adults with a disability, 28%); 1 mark for making a valid comparison using figures (e.g. adults with a disability participate at 28% compared to 61% for men aged 18-30); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (disabled adults face the greatest barriers to meeting recommended activity levels); 1 mark for suggesting one valid reason (inaccessible facilities; lack of adapted sessions or equipment; negative stereotypes about disabled people and sport; attitudinal barriers from coaches or institutions).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why socio-economic factors reduce participation in physical activity for young people. Give a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 marks per reason, must give 2 distinct reasons).
1 mark for identifying a valid socio-economic barrier; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism or giving a sporting example.
Acceptable answers: cost of club membership means families on lower incomes cannot afford organised sport (1) — for example, a young person wanting to play tennis may be unable to afford club fees, court hire and specialist coaching (1); lower disposable income means families cannot afford specialist equipment such as swimming kit, football boots or a bicycle (1) — this prevents participation at club and competitive level (1); lack of affordable facilities in lower-income neighbourhoods limits access to sport even if the individual wants to participate (1) — free community programmes are critical for equitable access (1).

practice_questions.text: A county sports partnership is trying to increase participation in sport among women aged 18-35 in a predominantly rural area. Analyse the range of factors that reduce participation for this group and the strategies the partnership could use to address them.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and develops at least three distinct barriers relevant to this specific group (gender + rural + age + likely socio-economic overlap). Applies each barrier to the sporting context and explains the mechanism. Discusses all three participation strategies (promotion, provision, access) with specific examples. Uses accurate terminology (sexism, stereotyping, DCMS, NGB, provision). Continuous analytical prose.

Secure: Addresses at least two barriers with some development and at least two strategies. Some sporting application. Generally accurate.

Developing: Relevant points but treated superficially. May list factors without explaining how they reduce participation. Limited strategy discussion.

Emerging: Basic observations. Little development or application to this specific group.

Acceptable barriers: sexism and stereotyping (sport seen as male domain, limiting female aspiration); limited media coverage of women's sport reducing role model visibility; family/caring commitments reducing leisure time; rural environment limiting access to facilities; cost of travel to distant facilities; lack of female-specific sessions or clubs locally.
Acceptable strategies: promotion (awareness campaigns challenging stereotypes, female role model ambassadors); provision (creating sessions at accessible times, establishing women-only sessions, funding local facility development); access (subsidising membership, providing childcare at sessions, scheduling around school hours).

before.exam_tip_html: On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question about engagement patterns, you must do three things: quote a specific figure from the data, make a comparison, and explain what it shows in a sporting context. Simply reading a number earns nothing — the mark scheme rewards the inference. For example: “Disabled students participate at 22% compared to 68% for male students — a gap of 46 percentage points — suggesting significant access or inclusion barriers for this group at this school.” On a 6 marks — Analyse question, avoid listing factors one by one. Instead, develop each point: name the factor, explain the mechanism, give a specific sporting example. A common error is addressing only one group. The spec requires knowledge of multiple social groups — aim to discuss at least two contrasting groups with specific barriers for each.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the golden triangle in sport?
A) The three phases of athletic training: strength, endurance and speed
B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media
C) The three main types of sports facilities: indoor, outdoor and aquatic
D) The three tiers of sports governance: local, national and international
practice_questions.marks: B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'commercialisation' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition indicating that sport is treated as a product or business; 1 mark for linking this to financial gain or profit, or to the involvement of sponsors, media or businesses. Example full-mark answer: 'Commercialisation is the process by which sport is treated as a commercial product, with businesses investing in it to generate profit through sponsorship, media rights and merchandise sales.'

practice_questions.text: State two types of sponsorship that a professional sports club might receive.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct types: financial sponsorship (1); clothing and equipment sponsorship (1); facility or venue sponsorship (1). Two answers describing the same type of financial support score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the estimated annual broadcast rights income (in millions of pounds) for four sports in the UK.

Sport | Annual broadcast rights income (£m)
Premier League football | 1,650
Rugby Union (Premiership) | 55
Women's Super League | 12
Athletics (UK events) | 8

Using the data in Table 1, interpret what this shows about the relationship between media coverage and commercialisation across these sports.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the sport with the highest broadcast income (Premier League football, £1,650m); 1 mark for a valid comparison using figures (e.g. Premier League income is over 130 times greater than Women's Super League income of £12m; or athletics earns only £8m compared to rugby's £55m); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (sports with larger television audiences attract greater broadcast income, which feeds into the golden triangle to attract more sponsorship and commercial partners); 1 mark for a relevant implication (less commercially broadcast sports receive less sponsorship income, leaving them under-resourced; or high broadcast income enables the Premier League to invest heavily in facilities, academies and coaching).

practice_questions.text: Explain two positive impacts and two negative impacts of sponsorship on performers in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any of the following, up to 4 marks total (must cover both positives and negatives for full marks).
Positive: financial security allowing full-time training (1); access to high-quality equipment and coaching (1); increased public profile through media exposure (1).
Negative: pressure to compete while injured to meet commercial obligations (1); loss of control over personal image as a brand ambassador (1); intense media scrutiny of personal life affecting mental wellbeing (1); risk of sudden loss of income if sponsor withdraws (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level hockey club has recently attracted a regional sports retailer as a kit sponsor. Analyse the impact of this sponsorship arrangement on the club, its players and the sponsoring company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses impacts on all three parties (club, players and sponsor) with developed points and specific examples. Considers both positive and negative implications for at least two parties. Uses accurate commercial vocabulary (sponsorship, branding, profile, obligations, golden triangle). Continuous analytical prose rather than a list.

Secure: Covers at least two of the three parties with developed points; mostly accurate; some sporting application.

Developing: Relevant points but limited development; may address only one party; minimal sporting context.

Emerging: Basic or vague points; no development; may only state that sponsorship provides money.

Acceptable points: Club gains kit and equipment costs covered and may attract better players (positive); club faces pressure to display sponsor logos prominently or associate with the brand (limitation); players gain professional-quality kit and raised local profile (positive); players may feel obligated to represent the brand positively off the pitch (constraint); sponsor gains brand visibility at matches and on player kit (positive); sponsor risks reputational damage if players behave badly (negative); sponsor reaches a targeted local audience of sport participants (commercial benefit).

practice_questions.text: Name the two bones that articulate at the hip joint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: femur and pelvis (both required for the mark).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ligament' and state its role in a synovial joint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining a ligament as a strong, elastic connective tissue; 1 mark for stating it connects bone to bone across a joint to provide stability and limit excessive movement.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of synovial fluid in a joint and explain how a warm-up improves its effectiveness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction between the articulating surfaces; 1 mark for stating that it nourishes the articular cartilage; 1 mark for explaining that during a warm-up, rising body temperature makes synovial fluid less viscous, allowing it to distribute more evenly and improving range of movement / reducing injury risk.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the shoulder joint allows a greater range of movement than the elbow joint, referring to joint type and the articulating bones at each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the shoulder as a ball-and-socket joint; 1 mark for explaining that the rounded head of the humerus fits into the socket of the scapula, allowing movement in all planes (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, circumduction); 1 mark for identifying the elbow as a hinge joint; 1 mark for explaining that the shape of the joint (humerus articulating with radius and ulna) restricts movement to flexion and extension in a single plane only.

practice_questions.text: State two types of movement that are available at a ball-and-socket joint but NOT at a hinge joint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two correct movements available at ball-and-socket joints only: abduction (moving a limb away from the midline), adduction (moving a limb towards the midline), rotation (turning the limb along its long axis), circumduction (circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction). Two near-identical answers (e.g. abduction and adduction described in the same way) are awarded 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level swimmer performs repeated overhead arm strokes during training. Analyse how the structures of the shoulder synovial joint support performance and reduce injury risk during this activity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least two structures discussed in detail with accurate physiological explanation; each structure linked specifically to the demands of overhead swimming (e.g. synovial fluid becoming less viscous during warm-up to allow the full range of circumduction required; ligaments stabilising the ball-and-socket joint against the repetitive shoulder rotation forces; articular cartilage absorbing compressive forces during the pull-through); technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Two structures identified and mostly accurately explained; applied to swimming in general terms; link between structure and performance present.

Developing: One or two structures named with limited explanation; sporting application vague.

Emerging: Basic naming of structures; little explanation of function or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: During a pull-up exercise, a gymnast bends her elbows to raise her body upward. Name the agonist muscle acting at the elbow joint during this upward phase.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: biceps.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'fixator' and give one sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for definition: a muscle that stabilises a joint or body part to allow another muscle to contract effectively, holding a bone still while movement occurs elsewhere; 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. the deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder during a bicep curl, keeping the upper arm stable while the elbow flexes / the abdominals act as fixators stabilising the pelvis during a sprint).

practice_questions.text: Describe the roles of the biceps, triceps and deltoid during the upward phase of a bicep curl.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating the biceps is the agonist, contracting to produce elbow flexion; 1 mark for stating the triceps is the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow the movement; 1 mark for stating the deltoid is the fixator at the shoulder joint, stabilising the upper arm throughout the movement.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the quadriceps and hamstrings work as an antagonistic pair during a football kick, including what happens in both the upswing and the follow-through.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the quadriceps as the agonist during knee extension (the upswing); 1 mark for explaining that the quadriceps contracts, shortening to straighten the knee and drive the foot towards the ball; 1 mark for identifying the hamstrings as the antagonist during the upswing, relaxing and lengthening to allow extension; 1 mark for explaining the role reversal on the follow-through: the hamstrings contract eccentrically (or as agonist) to decelerate the leg, acting as the prime mover for knee flexion to prevent over-extension and injury.

practice_questions.text: State two muscles from the OCR specification that are NOT in the biceps/triceps or quadriceps/hamstrings pairs, and state the primary action of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct muscle with its primary action. Accept any two from: deltoid (abduction of the arm at the shoulder), trapezius (elevation and retraction of the scapula / elevates shoulders), latissimus dorsi (extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder), pectorals (horizontal adduction of the arm / adducts the arm across the chest), abdominals (flexion of the spine / stabilises the trunk and pelvis), gluteals (extension of the hip), gastrocnemius (plantar flexion at the ankle). Two identical or near-identical answers score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A club-level badminton player performs a forehand smash. Analyse the roles of antagonistic muscle pairs and the fixator in producing this overhead striking action.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies at least two antagonistic pairs relevant to the smash (e.g. deltoid/latissimus dorsi at the shoulder; triceps/biceps at the elbow); each pair discussed in terms of agonist and antagonist roles anchored to specific phases of the smash; fixator named and its role explained (e.g. trapezius or abdominals as fixator stabilising the trunk or scapula); consistent sporting application throughout; technically accurate language.

Secure: Two pairs identified; mostly correct agonist/antagonist assignment; fixator mentioned; generally applied to the smash.

Developing: One pair discussed with development; or two pairs identified but fixator absent; sporting context present but superficial.

Emerging: Basic mention of agonist/antagonist with little development; fixator missing or incorrect; limited sporting application.

Acceptable content: at the shoulder, the deltoid (agonist) abducts and flexes to raise the arm; the latissimus dorsi and pectorals act as antagonists; at the elbow, the triceps (agonist) extends the elbow to produce the striking action; the biceps acts as the antagonist; the trapezius and abdominals act as fixators stabilising the scapula and trunk respectively.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes gamesmanship?
A) Behaviour that involves physically harming an opponent to gain advantage
B) Strategies that break the formal rules of the sport to achieve a result
C) Actions that are within the rules but deliberately violate the spirit of competition
D) Behaviour that shows respect and generosity towards opponents
practice_questions.marks: C) Actions that are within the rules but deliberately violate the spirit of competition [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sportsmanship' in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition identifying fair play, respect or generosity; 1 mark for linking this to treatment of opponents, officials or the rules of the sport. Example full-mark answer: 'Sportsmanship is behaviour that shows fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents, officials and the rules of the sport, placing the spirit of competition above personal gain.'

practice_questions.text: State two examples of etiquette from two different sports.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct examples from different sports. Examples: tennis player acknowledging a net cord to their opponent (1); golfer repairing a divot or raking a bunker (1); cricketer applauding a well-played innings by an opposition batsman (1); rugby player helping an opponent to their feet after a tackle (1); footballer kicking the ball into touch when an opponent is injured (1). Two examples from the same sport describing the same type of behaviour score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'etiquette' in sport and give one specific sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying etiquette as unwritten rules or informal codes of conduct (not part of the official rule book); 1 mark for explaining that etiquette involves customs or traditions expected of participants; 1 mark for a valid specific sporting example. Example full-mark answer: 'Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct expected of performers in sport (1). It consists of customs and traditions that are not part of the official rules but that participants are expected to follow to show respect for the sport and its opponents (1). For example, in tennis it is expected that a player will gesture to acknowledge a lucky net cord, even though there is no rule requiring this (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why performers might engage in deviant behaviour in sport. Give a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 marks per reason, must give 2 distinct reasons; 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development or example).
Acceptable reasons: to gain an unfair advantage (1) - for example, a power athlete using anabolic steroids to increase muscle mass and improve performance in competition (1); peer pressure within a sporting culture that normalises unethical behaviour (1) - for example, a young player who adopts aggressive fouling tactics because it is normalised and rewarded within their club culture (1); a win-at-all-costs culture driven by financial rewards, sponsorship or media pressure (1) - for example, a professional player who feigns injury to waste time and secure a narrow lead because the financial incentive of winning outweighs ethical concerns (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level netball player watches her team's opponents using repeated gamesmanship during a closely contested match, including deliberate time-wasting on restarts and persistent verbal comments designed to distract players at set pieces. Analyse the impact this behaviour might have on the match, the performers involved and the wider sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis across all three areas (match, performers, wider sport). Points are developed with specific examples from a sporting context. The distinction between gamesmanship and deviance is maintained. Uses accurate vocabulary (etiquette, sportsmanship, deviance, spirit of competition). Continuous analytical prose rather than a list.

Secure: Covers at least two of the three areas with developed points; mostly accurate; mostly applied to a sporting context.

Developing: Relevant points present but limited development; may address only one area; minimal sporting context.

Emerging: Basic observations that gamesmanship is bad; no development or application.

Acceptable points:
On the match: time-wasting reduces the quality of play and genuine competition time (negative); it may frustrate the opposition into making errors or receiving cautions (tactical gain for the gamesmanship team).
On the performers: players receiving gamesmanship may feel demoralised, distracted or become aggressive in response (negative); players using gamesmanship risk losing focus on their own game (self-harm); young performers may normalise this as acceptable behaviour (wider harm to sport culture).
On the wider sport: frequent gamesmanship erodes the spectator experience and reduces public enjoyment (negative); it undermines sport's role as a model of positive values for young participants (social harm); officials face greater difficulty managing the game (increased pressure on officiating); if it becomes culturally accepted, the spirit and values of netball are undermined long-term.

practice_questions.text: Which class of lever operates at the neck during nodding of the head?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: first class lever.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'mechanical advantage' as it applies to lever systems in the body.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining it is a measure of how much a lever amplifies force compared to the effort applied; 1 mark for linking it to the relative lengths of the effort arm and load arm (when the effort arm is longer than the load arm, mechanical advantage is greater than 1 and force is amplified; when the load arm is longer, MA is less than 1 and speed / range is amplified).

practice_questions.text: Describe the second class lever used at the ankle during a calf raise (plantar flexion). Name all three components and their positions.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the fulcrum as the ball of the foot (the pivot point at the toes); 1 mark for identifying the load as the body weight acting through the ankle joint (in the middle between the fulcrum and the effort); 1 mark for identifying the effort as the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles pulling via the Achilles tendon at the heel (at the far end from the fulcrum, with the load between them). Full credit requires the correct second class arrangement (load between fulcrum and effort).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the third class lever at the elbow produces less mechanical advantage than the second class lever at the ankle, and what sporting benefit this provides.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining that in the third class elbow lever, the effort arm (elbow to biceps insertion) is shorter than the load arm (elbow to hand), giving a mechanical advantage less than 1; 1 mark for stating this means the biceps must produce more force than the load being lifted; 1 mark for explaining the benefit: a small shortening of the biceps produces a large movement of the hand, amplifying speed and range of movement; 1 mark for applying to sport (e.g. this allows a thrower to generate high hand speed in throwing or striking actions, which is more useful than force amplification in these skills).

practice_questions.text: State two different sporting movements and identify the lever class operating at the main joint in each. For each movement, state whether the lever has a mechanical advantage greater or less than 1 and what this means for performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correctly described first movement with accurate lever class and a statement about mechanical advantage (e.g. calf raise at ankle = second class lever, MA greater than 1, force amplified, allows the calf muscles to lift body weight efficiently); 1 mark for a second, clearly different movement with accurate lever class and mechanical advantage statement (e.g. bicep curl at elbow = third class lever, MA less than 1, speed amplified, produces fast forearm movement useful for throwing / striking).

practice_questions.text: A school PE teacher argues that the body's reliance on third class levers in throwing and striking puts athletes at a mechanical disadvantage. Evaluate this view, considering the performance benefits and limitations of third class levers in sport compared with second class levers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of both lever classes; multiple sporting examples applied accurately; candidate clearly explains that third class levers do produce a mechanical disadvantage (effort arm shorter than load arm, MA less than 1, muscles must exert greater force than the load) but that this disadvantage is compensated by amplification of speed and range of movement; explains that second class levers (ankle in a calf raise) amplify force (MA greater than 1) but at the cost of speed; evaluates why the body needs both types for different functions; reaches a balanced conclusion acknowledging that ‘disadvantage’ is context-dependent — in striking and throwing sports, speed at the end of the limb is the goal, so third class levers are optimal for those tasks.

Secure: Both lever classes discussed with sporting examples; mostly accurate mechanical advantage explanations; conclusion reached; some balance in the argument.

Developing: One lever class discussed more thoroughly; limited comparison; sporting examples present but may not be precisely anchored to the body location.

Emerging: Basic description of lever classes; minimal evaluation of mechanical advantage or sporting application.

Agreeing with the teacher: third class levers (elbow in bicep curl, throwing action) do require the muscle to exert force greater than the load; MA less than 1 is technically a mechanical disadvantage; greater muscular effort is needed compared with a second class lever producing the same outcome.

Disagreeing / qualification: the ‘disadvantage’ in force production is traded for speed and range at the end of the limb; a javelin thrower’s hand speed is what determines throw distance — a second class lever at the elbow would produce greater force but far less speed; third class levers dominate the body because speed and range outweigh force requirements in most striking, catching and throwing sports; both lever types are essential — the ankle’s second class lever provides the force to drive the whole body off the ground; the elbow’s third class lever provides the speed to deliver a fast punch or throw.

practice_questions.text: Identify the category of performance-enhancing drug most likely to be used by a competitive archer wanting to reduce their heart rate during competition.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: beta blockers (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'stimulants' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that stimulants increase alertness or reduce fatigue; 1 mark for linking this to improved competitive performance or naming a side effect. Example full-mark answer: 'Stimulants are drugs that increase alertness, reduce fatigue and heighten competitiveness, giving performers in high-speed or combat sports a performance advantage, though they are prohibited in competition and carry side effects including elevated heart rate and risk of cardiac arrest.'

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the percentage of tested athletes in three sports who returned a positive test for prohibited substances in an international governing body's annual anti-doping report.

Sport | Positive test rate
Weightlifting | 3.8%
Archery | 1.2%
Athletics | 2.1%

Using the data in Table 1, calculate the difference in positive test rate between weightlifting and archery. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working (3.8% - 1.2%); 1 mark for the correct answer (2.6); 1 mark for the correct unit (percentage points or %). Full-mark answer: '3.8% - 1.2% = 2.6 percentage points. Weightlifting has a positive test rate 2.6 percentage points higher than archery.'

practice_questions.text: Using Table 1 above, interpret what the data shows about PED use across the three sports and suggest one reason why the highest rate appears in weightlifting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying weightlifting as having the highest positive test rate (3.8%); 1 mark for a valid comparison using figures (e.g. weightlifting's rate is more than three times that of archery at 1.2%); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (PED misuse is more prevalent in strength-based sports where physical power is a direct determinant of performance); 1 mark for a valid reason linked to the nature of the sport (anabolic steroids benefit power and strength athletes by increasing muscle mass and reducing recovery time, making the potential gain much greater in weightlifting than in precision or technical sports).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a professional performer might choose to use anabolic steroids, and two negative consequences of this decision.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 reasons + 2 consequences; must cover both for full marks, 1 mark per point).
Reasons: increased muscle mass improving strength and power performance (1); faster recovery from training enabling greater training volume (1); pressure from peers or coaching culture to use substances to keep up with competitors (1); financial incentive of competition success through prize money or sponsorship (1).
Negative consequences: risk of liver damage or cardiovascular disease (1); hormonal disruption affecting secondary sexual characteristics (1); if detected, receives a competition ban, fines and loss of medals (1); permanent reputational damage affecting future career and sponsorship (1).

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level sprinter is told by a senior teammate that 'everyone uses stimulants to get an edge at the top level' and that testing is rarely carried out at county competitions. Evaluate the arguments for and against the sprinter using stimulants, and reach a conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation presenting genuine arguments on both sides. Uses accurate physiological vocabulary (alertness, reduced fatigue, heart rate, side effects). Challenges the 'everyone does it' reasoning with counter-arguments. Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Consistent sporting application. Arguments are developed, not just listed.

Secure: Covers arguments for and against; mostly accurate physiological understanding; generally balanced; mostly applied to an athletic context; conclusion present.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or acknowledges both sides without developing either; some relevant points but underdeveloped; limited sporting application.

Emerging: Basic statements about drugs being good or bad; no physiological explanation; descriptive rather than evaluative.

Acceptable arguments for: stimulants increase alertness and reduce fatigue, directly improving sprint performance (1); may level the perceived playing field if the sprinter believes others are using them (1); low perceived risk of detection at county level reduces fear of sanction (1).
Arguments against: stimulants carry real health risks including elevated heart rate, anxiety and in extreme cases cardiac arrest - especially dangerous in a young person (1); the 'everyone does it' argument is flawed: many competitors do not use PEDs, so use creates an unfair disadvantage for clean athletes, not a level field (1); if detected at any level, consequences include a ban, loss of results and a permanent record that could affect future opportunities (1); drug use violates the principles of fair competition and the spirit of sport, causing reputational harm even if not detected (1); the teammate's claim is ethically inappropriate - peer pressure of this kind is one of the key reasons young performers are drawn into deviant behaviour, and the sprinter has the right to refuse (1).
Conclusion: stimulant use is both ethically wrong and practically risky; the short-term performance gain is outweighed by health risks, the unreliability of the 'level playing field' argument, and the long-term consequences for the sprinter's career and integrity.

practice_questions.text: Identify one cause of player violence in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one valid cause: frustration (1); rivalry (1); alcohol or drugs (1); disputed officiating decisions (1); win-at-all-costs culture (1); intimidation as a deliberate strategy (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'player violence' in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it involves aggressive physical or verbal behaviour by a performer; 1 mark for linking this to behaviour that goes beyond the accepted rules or norms of the sport. Example full-mark answer: 'Player violence is aggressive physical or verbal behaviour by a performer that goes beyond the accepted rules and norms of the sport, intending to harm or intimidate an opponent or official.'

practice_questions.text: State two causes of player violence in sport that are different from frustration.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct causes (excluding frustration as stated in the question). Acceptable answers: rivalry or the high stakes of the contest (1); alcohol or drugs reducing impulse control (1); disputed officiating decisions triggering a sense of injustice (1); win-at-all-costs culture encouraging intimidation (1); retaliation against an opponent (1). Two answers describing the same underlying cause score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe how rivalry between two teams or performers can lead to player violence. Give a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for explaining what rivalry is (an intense competitive relationship with high emotional stakes); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (elevated emotional investment lowers inhibitions, making performers more likely to commit a violent act they would avoid in a routine fixture); 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. ice hockey clubs with a long history of confrontation, or rugby players reacting aggressively in a high-stakes cup final that would not happen in a friendly). Example full-mark answer: 'Rivalry is an intense competitive relationship between two teams or performers where winning carries exceptional significance (1). In a high-stakes encounter such as a cup final or historic derby, the emotional pressure is so great that performers may react violently to provocation that they would absorb without incident in a routine fixture (1). For example, in ice hockey, club rivalries have historically produced violent confrontations between players that go beyond the regulated physical contact of the sport (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain how alcohol and drugs can cause player violence. Explain the impact this has on the sport involved.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 marks for cause, 2 marks for impact; or 4 single marks as below).
Cause: alcohol and drugs impair cognitive function and reduce impulse control (1); this lowers the psychological inhibitions that normally prevent aggressive behaviour, making performers more likely to react violently to a provocation (1).
Impact on sport: repeated violent incidents damage the sport's public image, reducing its appeal to families and potential new participants (1); governing bodies must respond with disciplinary procedures that divert resources and attention away from developing the sport (1); or: violence deters officials from continuing, creating shortages of qualified referees which harms the ability to run competitions safely (1).

practice_questions.text: A female county-level rugby player has witnessed a significant increase in dangerous late tackles and verbal abuse of officials in her division this season, which she links to intense rivalries between clubs competing for promotion. Analyse the range of factors that could explain the increase in player violence and the impact it is having on performers, officials and the sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and develops at least three distinct causes relevant to this context (rivalry/high stakes, frustration, win-at-all-costs culture; alcohol/drugs could also feature). Analyses the impact across all three groups (performers, officials, sport) with specific examples. Uses accurate vocabulary (frustration, rivalry, deviance, officiating decisions, inhibitions). Continuous analytical prose rather than a list.

Secure: Addresses at least two causes with development and discusses at least two of the three impact groups. Some sporting application. Generally accurate.

Developing: Relevant points but limited development. May list causes without explaining mechanisms. Impact discussion limited to one group. Minimal sporting context.

Emerging: Basic observations about violence being bad. No development of causes or impact. No sporting application.

Acceptable causes: rivalry and promotion pressure elevating emotional stakes (developed with rugby example); frustration building over repeated foul play or unfair decisions; win-at-all-costs culture within clubs encouraging intimidation as a tactical strategy; perceived injustice from officiating decisions triggering retaliation.
Acceptable impacts: performers face bans, injury risk and reputational damage; officials face verbal and physical abuse making their role untenable, deterring recruitment; the sport suffers reputational damage that deters spectators, sponsors and young participants, undermining rugby's values of physical contact within disciplined rules.

practice_questions.text: Identify the plane of movement used during a forward somersault.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: sagittal plane.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'longitudinal axis'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a vertical axis; 1 mark for stating it runs from the top of the head to the feet (or through the spine vertically) and that the body rotates around it during spinning or twisting actions (e.g. a 360 degree turn in ice skating).

practice_questions.text: Describe the plane and axis of movement used when a gymnast performs a cartwheel. Include the direction of movement in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the frontal plane; 1 mark for identifying the frontal axis (do NOT accept 'sagittal axis' — this is not OCR terminology); 1 mark for describing the direction of movement as side-to-side (the body tips laterally over the hands, moving away from the midline).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a discus thrower spinning in a full circle before release uses the transverse plane and longitudinal axis rather than any other plane-and-axis combination.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating the movement is a horizontal rotation or spin; 1 mark for identifying the transverse plane (which divides the body into upper and lower halves); 1 mark for identifying the longitudinal axis (which runs vertically from head to feet); 1 mark for explaining that because the thrower rotates around a vertical axis rather than forwards/backwards or side-to-side, neither the sagittal nor frontal planes apply.

practice_questions.text: State two joint movements that occur in the sagittal plane, and give a sporting example of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct movement with a valid sporting example. Accept: flexion (e.g. bending the knee during a squat / bringing the thigh forward in running); extension (e.g. straightening the knee during a kick / the follow-through of a throw). Both answers must name the movement and give a sporting context. Two near-identical examples of the same movement (e.g. two examples of flexion) score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A sports science student is asked to analyse the movement of a figure skater performing a spin followed by a jump that involves a forward somersault rotation. Analyse how the planes and axes of movement change between the spin and the somersault.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly identifies the transverse plane and longitudinal axis for the spin, with explanation that the body rotates horizontally around a vertical axis; clearly identifies the sagittal plane and transverse axis for the forward somersault, with explanation that the body rotates forward around a side-to-side axis; analyses what changes between the two movements (rotation shifts from vertical/longitudinal axis during the spin to horizontal/transverse axis during the somersault); links both to how coaching cues could reinforce the correct axis (e.g. for the spin the coach would cue the athlete to keep their longitudinal axis straight; for the somersault they would cue tucking to increase rotation speed around the transverse axis). Sustained sporting application throughout.

Secure: Correctly identifies both plane-axis pairs; some explanation of direction of rotation; limited or inconsistent application to coaching.

Developing: One plane-axis pair correctly identified; basic description of direction of movement; little or no coaching application.

Emerging: One relevant term used (plane or axis) with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a closed skill?
A) A basketball player receiving a bounce pass from a teammate during a fast break
B) A gymnast performing a vault on a consistent, controlled run-up
C) A tennis player returning a serve from an opponent
D) A rugby scrum-half passing after receiving a ball from a maul
practice_questions.marks: B) A gymnast performing a vault on a consistent, controlled run-up [1 mark]. The environment is stable and predictable; the movement can be pre-planned and repeated identically. All other options involve unpredictable, changing environments (open skills).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'open skill' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: a skill performed in an unpredictable or changing environment. 1 mark for development: the performer must adapt their movement continuously to respond to changes in the situation (accept: opponents, teammates, or external conditions change and the performer reacts to them). Do not credit definitions that describe open skills as difficult or unstructured.

practice_questions.text: Describe three characteristics of skilful movement, using a sporting example for each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each characteristic correctly described with a brief sporting example (up to 3 marks). Accept any three of: efficiency — no wasted energy or movement, e.g. an elite swimmer using a high elbow pull to maximise propulsion without excess drag (1); pre-determined — the performer has a clear intended outcome before executing, e.g. a netball shooter visualising the arc before releasing (1); co-ordinated — body parts work in correct sequence, e.g. the approach, hip drive and arm action of a javelin throw combining in a timed chain (1); fluent — movement flows smoothly without pausing, e.g. an experienced breaststroke swimmer blending the pull and kick phases seamlessly (1); aesthetic — the movement is pleasing to observe, e.g. a curved finish shot curling into the top corner (1). Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: A football coach watches a Year-7 pupil attempt a long pass and notices jerky, hesitant movement with wasted arm tension. Explain how this contrasts with the characteristics of skilful movement shown by an elite midfielder.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for identifying weaknesses in the beginner: movement is not fluent (pausing/jerking between sub-routines) (1); energy is wasted through excess muscle tension, so it lacks efficiency (1). Up to 2 marks for linking to characteristics shown by the elite player: the elite midfielder's movement is fluent — phases blend seamlessly (1); it is efficient — only the required muscles fire in the correct sequence, conserving energy (1). Accept references to co-ordinated or pre-determined with appropriate sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A county athletics coach is classifying the discus throw and the 100-metre hurdles on OCR's two skill continua. Analyse the placement of each event on both continua, justifying your answers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses both skills on both continua (four placements total) with clear, definition-based justifications. Discus throw — simple/complex: towards the complex end; requires co-ordination of approach, spin, hip drive, arm swing and release angle, multiple sub-routines demanding simultaneous control (1); open/closed: towards the closed end during competition; the circle is a fixed, controlled environment and the performer initiates when ready, with no opposition interfering (1). Hurdles — simple/complex: more complex than a flat sprint, as the athlete must time the take-off, lead leg clearance and trail leg mechanics for each barrier (1); open/closed: towards the closed end; the hurdles are fixed positions, the track is constant, the environment is predictable (1). Strong responses note that both events are towards the closed end of the environmental continuum but differ on the difficulty continuum. Consistent use of continuum terminology and definitions throughout.

Secure: Correctly places both events on at least three of the four continuum positions, with mostly accurate justifications. May be less precise on one placement.

Developing: Places each event on one continuum only, or gives correct labels without justification. Some continuum terminology used.

Emerging: Names the continua without placing either skill; or confuses the two continua definitions.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club swimmer competes in both sprint freestyle events and open-water swimming races. Evaluate the view that the two OCR skill continua give a complete and useful picture of how these two activities differ as sporting skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, each applied to the swimming scenario, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the two continua do capture key differences — pool sprint freestyle is towards the closed end (predictable lane, no opponents to dodge) but open-water racing sits further open (currents, other competitors' position, turns around buoys vary); the difficulty continuum distinguishes the more complex demands of open-water navigation (multiple environmental stimuli to process) from the more straightforward cyclic arm-pull pattern of pool freestyle; using the continua helps coaches design appropriate training — pool training can be highly repetitive/closed-skill-focused, while open-water prep needs open-skill adaptability drills. Arguments against: two continua cannot fully capture all distinctions between sports; the five characteristics of skilful movement add a dimension the continua miss (e.g. efficiency differences between the two settings); other factors such as fitness level, pacing strategy and tactics are not addressed by skill classification; the placement on a continuum is somewhat subjective and may vary with the specific race conditions. Justified conclusion: the two continua are a useful starting framework for comparing skills but should be used alongside other analytical tools for a complete picture.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the swimming scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; may focus on one swimmer only; thin sporting application.

Emerging: One-sided or very basic response; little or no sporting application to the scenario.

practice_questions.text: Name the vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: pulmonary vein.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'cardiac output'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying cardiac output as the total volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute; 1 mark for stating it is calculated as stroke volume multiplied by heart rate (or giving the formula Q = SV × HR).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows data for a trained cyclist at rest and during a 20-minute time trial.

Condition      | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
At rest        | 48               | 85
During race    | 172              | 115

Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the time trial. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct resting cardiac output with working shown: Q = 48 × 85 = 4,080 ml/min; 1 mark for correct exercise cardiac output with working shown: Q = 172 × 115 = 19,780 ml/min; 1 mark for including correct units (ml/min or equivalent L/min) on both answers. If method is correct but arithmetic is wrong, award 1 mark for the correct formula and substitution.

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old club swimmer's heart rate data is recorded during a training set. Resting: 62 bpm. End of warm-up: 105 bpm. Peak (mid-set): 178 bpm. Five minutes after finishing: 88 bpm.

Interpret what the data tells you about how the cardiovascular system responds during and after the swim set.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the increase in heart rate from rest to peak (116 bpm rise) and stating that this reflects the increased demand for oxygen from the working muscles; 1 mark for explaining that stroke volume also increases during exercise, meaning cardiac output rises substantially; 1 mark for identifying the recovery drop (from 178 bpm to 88 bpm within 5 minutes) and linking this to the body's return towards its resting state; 1 mark for a valid sporting interpretation (e.g. the large rise in heart rate confirms the high oxygen demand of competitive swimming; the drop in recovery heart rate suggests the swimmer is reasonably well conditioned). If calculations are used, show working and units.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the bicuspid, tricuspid and semilunar valves in the pathway of blood through the heart.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining the tricuspid valve: located between the right atrium and right ventricle; prevents blood flowing back from the right ventricle into the right atrium; 1 mark for explaining the bicuspid valve: located between the left atrium and left ventricle; prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium; 1 mark for explaining the semilunar valves: located at the exit of each ventricle (into the aorta and pulmonary artery); prevent backflow into the ventricles between beats; 1 mark for correctly placing all three in the sequence of blood flow through the heart. Accept equivalent anatomical descriptions.

practice_questions.text: A county-level middle-distance runner is preparing for a 12-week pre-season training block. Evaluate the importance of an efficient cardiovascular system to her performance in a competitive 800 m race, considering both heart structure and the pathway of blood.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Full range of relevant cardiovascular content applied consistently to 800 m racing. Includes: double-circulatory system (pulmonary and systemic loops) enabling continuous oxygen delivery; named valves preventing backflow ensuring one-directional flow; cardiac output calculation linked to exercise demand (heart rate and stroke volume both rising during the race); red blood cells transporting oxygen to the quadriceps and gastrocnemius during the race effort; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles; long-term training adaptations (cardiac hypertrophy, increased stroke volume, lower resting heart rate) that improve efficiency. Evaluation includes both sides: the value of a highly efficient cardiovascular system vs the constraints (genetic ceiling on maximum cardiac output; lactic acid accumulation in the final stages regardless of cardiovascular fitness). Justified conclusion about whether cardiovascular efficiency is the most important limiting factor for 800 m performance. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): Most cardiovascular structures and responses covered with reasonable accuracy; applied to the 800 m context; evaluation of at least two relevant points; conclusion reached; some minor inaccuracies or undeveloped sections.

Developing (2 marks): Cardiovascular structures described with limited application to the 800 m race; cardiac output mentioned but not calculated or applied; one-sided.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic points about heart rate increasing during exercise; limited structure or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Identify one reason why an athlete would use goal setting during a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of the following: to support exercise/training adherence (keep the athlete returning to training consistently) (1); to motivate the performer by giving them a reference point for progress (1); to improve and/or optimise performance by providing a structured target (1). Do not credit vague answers such as 'to help them train' without specifying which of the three purposes.

practice_questions.text: State two features of a SMART target that help a performer track their progress.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct features: measurable — progress can be tracked using objective data such as times or distances (1); recorded — the goal is written down so it can be reviewed and monitored over time (1); timed — a deadline provides a natural review point (1). Maximum 2 marks; do not credit the same idea twice with different wording.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a SMART target in physical education.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly named and briefly explained element, up to 3 marks. Accept any three of: Specific — the goal is precisely defined with no ambiguity (1); Measurable — progress can be tracked using numbers or objective data (1); Achievable — the goal is challenging but realistic given the performer's current ability (1); Recorded — the goal is written down and documented for monitoring (1); Timed — the goal has a clear deadline (1). The letter A in OCR SMART stands for Achievable and R for Recorded — credit these terms or correct descriptions.

practice_questions.text: A club hockey player has written the following goal: 'Improve at hockey this season.' Explain why this goal does not meet the SMART criteria, and rewrite it as a SMART target.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for the critique: the goal is not specific — it does not state which aspect of hockey performance is to be improved (1); it is not measurable — there is no objective data to track whether improvement has occurred (1); it is not timed — no deadline is given (1); it is not recorded as a formal target (1). Maximum 2 for the critique. Up to 2 marks for the rewrite: a rewritten goal that includes a specific and measurable element (e.g. 'increase my penalty corner conversion rate from 30% to 45%') (1); and at least two further SMART elements (achievable context, recorded in training log, timed deadline) (1). Accept valid alternative sport-specific targets.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a county-level badminton player could use the SMART principle to set a goal that supports both their motivation and their long-term performance improvement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses all five SMART elements with explanation of each linked to both motivation and performance improvement in a badminton context. Points might include: Specific — 'increase first-serve accuracy to 70%' gives the player a precise focus for training, directing effort to the right technical area (1); Measurable — recording first-serve percentages each session shows the gap closing, which itself motivates by demonstrating progress (1); Achievable — a realistic target prevents demotivation from repeated failure; an unachievable target would reduce training adherence (1); Recorded — logging the goal and weekly measurements creates accountability and a narrative of progress (1); Timed — 'by the county championships in 8 weeks' creates urgency, allows the coach to structure progressive weekly drills (1). Strong responses link each element to both motivation and performance improvement explicitly, rather than treating them as separate. May note that the recorded element also helps the coach adapt sessions if progress stalls.

Secure: At least four SMART elements explained with mostly accurate links to the badminton context. Mentions both motivation and performance but may not connect them consistently.

Developing: Names at least three SMART elements with some explanation. Limited link to motivation or performance improvement. May simply list without analysing.

Emerging: Names SMART letters without explaining them; little or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Write a full SMART target for a 16-year-old club javelin thrower whose current personal best is 31 metres, preparing for the county championship in nine weeks.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific and measurable element: e.g. 'throw a minimum of 35 metres' — a named distance improvement at the named event (1). 1 mark for the achievable element with context: a 4-metre improvement in nine weeks is achievable for a county-level athlete with twice-weekly coaching sessions (1). 1 mark for timed and recorded: 'by the county championship in 9 weeks, recorded in training log and reviewed weekly with the coach' (1). Accept alternative distances or timelines provided they are internally consistent. Do not credit 'Accepted' or 'Realistic' as the OCR terms for A and R.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct order of the air pathway from the trachea to the site of gaseous exchange?
A) Trachea → alveoli → bronchi → bronchioles
B) Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
C) Trachea → bronchioles → bronchi → alveoli
D) Trachea → alveoli → bronchioles → bronchi
practice_questions.marks: B) Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'tidal volume'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying tidal volume as a measure of air volume per breath; 1 mark for specifying it is the volume inhaled or exhaled in a single normal breath (accept: approximately 0.5 litres at rest).

practice_questions.text: State two muscles involved in breathing and describe the role of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming the diaphragm and stating it contracts and flattens during inhalation, increasing chest volume to draw air in; 1 mark for naming the intercostal muscles and stating they raise the rib cage upward and outward during inhalation (or: relax and lower the rib cage during exhalation). Accept either inhalation or exhalation descriptions for intercostals, provided they are accurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe three structural features of the alveoli that make gaseous exchange efficient.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: large surface area of the alveoli; moist, thin walls (one cell thick); short diffusion distance/pathway; large capillary network surrounding the alveoli; large blood supply; concentration gradient is maintained (oxygen high in alveolus, low in blood; CO2 high in blood, low in alveolus). Accept equivalent wording.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club swimmer trains four days per week at high intensity. Explain how her breathing mechanics change during a maximal swim effort compared with breathing at rest.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that breathing rate increases during exercise; 1 mark for explaining that tidal volume increases (deeper breaths); 1 mark for naming an accessory inspiratory muscle (e.g. pectorals) that assists inhalation during intense exercise; 1 mark for explaining that abdominal muscles actively contract on exhalation to force air out more rapidly (compared with passive exhalation at rest). Partial credit: 3 marks for any three of these points accurately explained.

practice_questions.text: A county-level middle-distance runner is preparing for a regional 1500 m race. Analyse how the structure of the respiratory system allows her to maintain a sufficient supply of oxygen to her muscles throughout the race.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed, well-developed response that links several structural features of the respiratory system (alveolar structure, diffusion gradient, capillary network) to sustained oxygen delivery during the 1500 m. Each point is applied to the running context and explained mechanistically. Accurate use of terms such as diffusion, concentration gradient, haemoglobin, tidal volume and minute ventilation. OCR term 'breathing rate' used correctly.

Secure (3-4 marks): Most key points present and generally accurate. Structural features are identified and broadly linked to the race context, though some points may be stated rather than fully explained. Most technical vocabulary used correctly.

Developing (2 marks): Relevant points made about the pathway of air or alveolar features, but development is limited. May list features without explaining how they help the runner. Some inaccuracy in terminology.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic correct point about the respiratory system or breathing during exercise, with little or no application to the racing context.

practice_questions.text: Identify whether the following activity is aerobic or anaerobic: a swimmer completing a 50 m sprint at maximum effort in approximately 27 seconds.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: anaerobic. The very high intensity over under 30 seconds means oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough. Accept: anaerobic exercise / uses the anaerobic pathway. Do not accept 'aerobic'.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'anaerobic exercise'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that anaerobic exercise takes place without sufficient oxygen; 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down to produce energy and lactic acid as a by-product.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct differences: aerobic uses oxygen / anaerobic does not use sufficient oxygen; aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water / anaerobic produces lactic acid; aerobic can be sustained for longer / anaerobic is short duration; aerobic is lower intensity / anaerobic is very high intensity. Do not award two marks for the same physiological point expressed differently.

practice_questions.text: A county-level basketball player performs a 30-second burst of high-intensity court sprints and jumps during a training drill. Describe why lactic acid accumulates during this effort and what effect this has on the player.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the exercise intensity is too high for oxygen to be delivered fast enough, triggering anaerobic respiration; 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down without oxygen, producing lactic acid as a by-product; 1 mark for describing the consequence (lactic acid accumulates in the muscles and blood, causing fatigue and a burning sensation, limiting the player's ability to sustain the effort).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a 100 m sprinter and a 5,000 m runner require training for different energy systems, even though both are performing running events.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining that the 100 m sprint (approximately 10 seconds at maximal intensity) is predominantly anaerobic because the energy demand rate exceeds oxygen delivery capacity; 1 mark for stating the word equation for anaerobic respiration (glucose → energy + lactic acid); 1 mark for explaining that the 5,000 m (13+ minutes at sustained high intensity) is predominantly aerobic because oxygen delivery can keep pace with demand over the longer duration; 1 mark for stating the word equation for aerobic respiration (glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water) and linking to the sustained effort the aerobic system allows.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level hockey player competes in a 70-minute outdoor match. Evaluate which energy system — aerobic or anaerobic — is more important to her overall match performance, and how each contributes at different points in the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced, well-developed evaluation with consistent sporting application to hockey. Aerobic system: dominant during the majority of the match (jogging, sustained running, sustained press); defined correctly (glucose + oxygen → energy + CO2 + water); advantages — sustainable over 70 minutes, efficient energy production, supports cardiovascular endurance; supported by specific examples (maintaining pressing throughout the second half). Anaerobic system: dominant during explosive moments (sprinting to intercept a pass, penalty corner execution, tackling); defined correctly (glucose → energy + lactic acid); advantages — fast energy release for high-intensity bursts; limitations — lactic acid builds up, causes fatigue, cannot be sustained. Evaluation reaches a justified conclusion: aerobic system is more important overall due to the 70-minute duration, but anaerobic capacity determines performance in decisive moments. Both sides consistently anchored to hockey-specific examples.

Secure (3-4 marks): Both systems addressed with reasonable accuracy and applied to hockey; evaluation of both sides present; conclusion reached; some minor inaccuracies or undeveloped points.

Developing (2 marks): One system covered well, or both described with limited evaluation; sporting context present but limited; may not reach a clear conclusion.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic identification of aerobic or anaerobic with minimal development; little or no sporting application to hockey.

practice_questions.text: Identify one mental preparation technique a penalty taker in football might use in the moments before striking the ball.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of the following: imagery (1); mental rehearsal (1); selective attention (1); positive thinking (1). Accept brief descriptions that clearly identify one of the four named techniques. Do not credit arousal management, deep breathing or other techniques not on the OCR specification.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'selective attention' in the context of sporting performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: selective attention is the ability to focus on relevant information during performance. 1 mark for the second dimension: blocking out or filtering out irrelevant distractions (such as crowd noise, opponent behaviour or anxiety) that are not useful to the execution of the skill.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a county-level diver could use mental rehearsal to prepare for a new dive in competition.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that mental rehearsal involves running through the skill sequence internally before physical execution (1). 1 mark for describing the process: the diver runs through each phase of the dive in order (approach, hurdle step, take-off, tuck, entry) in real time, from a first-person perspective, picturing successful execution (1). 1 mark for the benefit: rehearsing the movement activates similar motor pathways to physical practice, reinforcing the movement programme and building familiarity without physical effort or injury risk (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how positive thinking could help a club-level rugby goal kicker maintain performance under pressure during a high-stakes conversion attempt.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that positive thinking involves replacing negative internal thoughts with prepared positive statements (1). 1 mark for the mechanism: negative thoughts (e.g. 'I always miss under pressure') are interrupted by a prepared positive script, redirecting attention from feared outcomes to execution cues (1). 1 mark for application: the kicker uses a statement such as 'I have practised this kick hundreds of times' or 'trust my technique' to maintain focus on the process (1). 1 mark for the outcome: confidence is maintained, muscles remain relaxed, and the execution cues rather than the outcome drive the performance (1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level gymnast is preparing for her first national competition. Her coach suggests she incorporates all four mental preparation techniques into her warm-up routine. Evaluate how effective each technique could be in helping her perform at her best.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation addressing all four techniques, considering both benefits and limitations for this gymnast scenario, with a justified conclusion. Arguments for imagery: creates multi-sensory familiarity with the competitive hall and the routine before physical execution, reducing the novelty of the competitive environment; limitation: requires skill to generate detailed imagery — a performer new to the technique may struggle to produce vivid, stable mental pictures. Arguments for mental rehearsal: activates motor pathways and reinforces the floor routine sequence without physical fatigue; first-competition nerves may cause rehearsal to be rushed or to drift to negative outcomes if not carefully managed. Arguments for selective attention: narrows focus to the floor and the music, filtering out judge presence and crowd noise — critical for a first national appearance; limitation: developing attention control takes time and practice; it cannot be fully acquired the week before competition. Arguments for positive thinking: interrupts performance anxiety and refocuses the gymnast on what she can do; limitation: statements must be believable — hollow reassurance collapses under real pressure. Conclusion: all four techniques contribute and they work best in combination; selective attention and positive thinking are most immediately deployable, while imagery and mental rehearsal require more practice to be fully effective. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure: Addresses at least three techniques with mostly developed points on both sides. Mostly applied to the gymnast scenario. Reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Addresses two or three techniques but one-sided (mostly benefits); thin application or limited development.

Emerging: Names one or two techniques; descriptive rather than evaluative; little sporting application.

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which imagery differs from mental rehearsal as mental preparation techniques.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct differences: imagery focuses on vivid multi-sensory experience (feelings, sounds, sights of the performance environment), while mental rehearsal is a structured run-through of the movement sequence (1); imagery creates mental familiarity with the competitive environment and emotional state, while mental rehearsal rehearses the exact procedural movement programme (1); imagery is broader and sensory, while mental rehearsal is procedural and movement-focused (1). Maximum 2 marks; do not credit the same distinction twice.

practice_questions.text: Identify one short-term effect of exercise on the cardiovascular system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: increased heart rate; increased stroke volume; increased cardiac output; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles. Accept equivalent physiological descriptions.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'capillarisation' as a long-term effect of exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying capillarisation as the growth of new capillaries in and around trained muscle tissue; 1 mark for stating that this increases capillary density and improves oxygen delivery to the muscle fibres (or: improves the removal of waste products such as CO2).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows resting heart rate data for three athletes before and after a 6-month endurance training programme.

Athlete | Resting HR before (bpm) | Resting HR after (bpm)
Amira   | 74                      | 59
Ben     | 70                      | 57
Chloe   | 76                      | 62

Calculate the mean reduction in resting heart rate across all three athletes. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly calculating each individual reduction (Amira: 15 bpm; Ben: 13 bpm; Chloe: 14 bpm); 1 mark for summing correctly (15 + 13 + 14 = 42 bpm) and dividing by 3; 1 mark for the correct final answer: 14 bpm (accept 14.0). Units required (bpm) for the final answer mark.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows heart rate and stroke volume data at rest and during a 10 km race for a trained distance runner.

Condition     | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
