At rest       | 52               | 88
During race   | 185              | 118

Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the race, and interpret what the data tells you about the runner's cardiovascular fitness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct resting cardiac output: Q = 52 × 88 = 4,576 ml/min; 1 mark for correct race cardiac output: Q = 185 × 118 = 21,830 ml/min; 1 mark for a valid comparison (e.g. cardiac output increases approximately 4.8 times during the race compared with rest, from 4,576 to 21,830 ml/min); 1 mark for a sporting interpretation (e.g. the low resting heart rate of 52 bpm suggests long-term cardiac hypertrophy, with a high stroke volume of 88 ml at rest indicating an efficient, trained heart capable of meeting the greatly elevated oxygen demand during the 10 km). If calculations are incorrect but method is sound, award 1 mark for working and 1 mark for a valid interpretation of their figures.

practice_questions.text: Explain how hypertrophy of the heart leads to a lower resting heart rate in a trained endurance athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining hypertrophy of the heart as the long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle due to regular training; 1 mark for explaining that this means the heart can pump a greater stroke volume per beat; 1 mark for explaining that a higher stroke volume means the heart beats fewer times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output; 1 mark for naming a lower resting heart rate as the result (accept: bradycardia; state that it is typically below 60 bpm in trained athletes). Full marks require the logical chain to be clear.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level netball player has been following a structured 8-month fitness programme. Evaluate the short-term and long-term effects this programme is likely to have had on her cardiovascular and respiratory systems, and explain how these effects could improve her performance on court.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Full range of short-term and long-term effects covered with accuracy. Short-term: increased heart rate/stroke volume/cardiac output during matches; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles; increased breathing rate and tidal volume; increased oxygen delivery; lactic acid production during explosive efforts. Long-term: hypertrophy of the heart; lower resting heart rate (with mechanism explained); increased resting stroke volume and cardiac output; capillarisation improving oxygen delivery to muscles; stronger respiratory muscles; improved aerobic capacity; better rate of recovery; improved resistance to fatigue. Each adaptation linked to a specific netball performance benefit (e.g. capillarisation supports sustained running in attack/defence; lower resting heart rate means she recovers faster between high-intensity passages of play; stronger respiratory muscles support higher minute ventilation during intense defensive sets). Evaluation includes at least one limitation or counter-argument (e.g. long-term adaptations take months and are reversible if training stops; short-term fatigue can temporarily impair performance; genetic ceiling on cardiac output). Justified conclusion.

Secure (3-4 marks): Most cardiovascular and respiratory effects covered with reasonable accuracy; most applied to netball; some evaluation; conclusion reached.

Developing (2 marks): Short-term or long-term effects described but not both; limited sporting application to netball; one-sided.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic reference to heart rate increasing during exercise or the heart getting bigger; limited application or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of guidance being used when a gymnastics coach physically moves a learner's arms through the correct cartwheel pattern.
practice_questions.marks: Manual guidance [1 mark]. The coach is physically assisting the performer's movement through direct physical contact, moving their body through the correct movement pattern.

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using visual guidance when coaching a beginner in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct advantages: it provides a complete mental image of the skill, giving beginners a blueprint of the correct movement pattern they have no prior experience of (1); video can be replayed, paused and slowed down for detailed analysis of each phase of the movement (1); it shows the whole skill in context, which is more meaningful than an abstract verbal description (1); it is easy to understand without requiring the performer to have prior knowledge of the technique (1). Maximum 2 marks; do not credit the same point with different wording.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a swimming coach could use mechanical guidance when teaching a beginner to swim front crawl, and explain one disadvantage of this approach.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for an accurate description of mechanical guidance in this context: the coach uses armbands, a float or a pull buoy to support the swimmer's body position, allowing them to focus on arm technique while the device provides buoyancy (1). 1 mark for identifying a disadvantage: the swimmer may develop dependency on the float or armbands (1). 1 mark for developing the disadvantage: without the aid the swimmer has not learned to manage their own buoyancy, which is a fundamental requirement for independent swimming; when the aid is removed they must still learn this element from scratch (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why verbal guidance is more effective for an elite javelin thrower than for a beginner attempting the event for the first time. Use your knowledge of how each performer uses memory in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for explaining effectiveness for the elite performer: the elite thrower has an established, detailed movement programme stored in long-term memory (1); a single precise verbal cue (e.g. 'release 3 degrees earlier') activates and fine-tunes this existing pattern, translating into a physical adjustment without disrupting the automatic flow of the skill (1). Up to 2 marks for explaining the limitation for the beginner: the beginner has no stored movement programme in long-term memory (1); they cannot translate abstract verbal instructions into co-ordinated physical movement without also seeing or physically experiencing the skill, so verbal guidance alone provides insufficient information for the beginner to perform correctly (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level athletics coach is deciding which types of guidance to use with two performers: a Year-7 beginner learning the shot put for the first time, and a county-level sixth-form athlete preparing for a regional championship. Analyse how the coach should use guidance differently for each performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least three guidance types across both performers, with clear justifications rooted in stage of learning and the sporting context. Distinguishes between the two performers consistently throughout. Might include: Visual guidance — for the beginner, a live demonstration of the correct put action provides the mental blueprint they lack; for the elite athlete, video analysis of their glide phase or release angle can identify subtle technical faults (1+1). Verbal guidance — limited use for the beginner because they lack an existing movement programme to attach cues to; highly effective for the elite athlete who can translate a brief technical cue ('extend the glide earlier') into a physical adjustment (1+1). Manual guidance — appropriate for the beginner to give the correct kinaesthetic feel for the stance and wrist position; inappropriate for the elite athlete as it disrupts the automatic motor programme they have developed over years (1+1). Mechanical guidance — a lighter shot or a marked circle could constrain the beginner's practice safely; elite athletes rarely need mechanical guidance for this event. Consistently evaluates rather than just listing.

Secure: Three guidance types discussed with mostly accurate justification. Distinguishes between performers on at least two types.

Developing: Two guidance types with some justification; less clear on why the distinction between beginner and elite exists.

Emerging: One or two types named with little justification; may not distinguish between performers.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club trampolinist is learning a new double somersault. Her coach uses a safety harness during the initial practice sessions. Evaluate whether mechanical guidance is always the most appropriate form of guidance when teaching new acrobatic skills, referring to both its benefits and limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on both sides, consistently applied to the trampolinist scenario and/or other acrobatic sporting examples, with a justified conclusion. Arguments in support of mechanical guidance: the safety harness allows the athlete to experience the correct rotation without risk of injury; the physical sensation from being supported through the skill provides information about body position that verbal description could not convey; it builds confidence so the performer is not held back by fear; it prevents the reinforcement of incorrect patterns by constraining the movement. Arguments against / limitations: over-reliance on the harness creates dependency — the trampolinist may fail to develop the internal body control needed to perform unsupported; the harness slightly alters the feel of the rotation so adjustment is still required when performing without it; other guidance types may be more effective in combination, such as verbal cues ('tuck tighter') and video analysis of unsupported attempts; for acrobatic skills at a lower danger level, visual or manual guidance may be equally effective without the dependency risk; mechanical guidance requires specialised equipment not always available in community settings. Justified conclusion: mechanical guidance is most appropriate in high-risk acrobatic skills during the early learning phase but should be progressively withdrawn as competence develops, combined with verbal and visual guidance for complete skill acquisition.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the trampolinist scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but underdeveloped; sporting context present but thin or predominantly one-sided.

Emerging: Basic response; may list guidance types without evaluating mechanical guidance specifically.

before.exam_tip_html: On 6-mark analyse questions about guidance, the most effective structure is: name the guidance type → explain its key feature → link it specifically to either a beginner or elite performer with a sporting example → justify why it suits that performer level. A common error is saying “visual guidance is good for beginners” without explaining why (beginners have no stored movement pattern to draw on, so seeing the skill demonstrated provides the mental blueprint they need). On the 6-mark evaluate question, always address both benefits and limitations of each guidance type, applying your points to the scenario. Read the scenario carefully — if the question specifies a beginner, the examiner wants to see why, for example, verbal guidance alone would be insufficient. Range of guidance types, balance (benefits and limitations) and consistent sporting application are what lift an answer into the top band.

practice_questions.text: Identify which type of feedback comes from within the performer's own body.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: intrinsic feedback (accept internal feedback).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'knowledge of performance'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that knowledge of performance is feedback about the quality or technique of a movement (not the outcome). 1 mark for development: it tells the performer what to correct in their technique rather than simply whether they succeeded or failed; or gives a sporting example (e.g. a coach telling a high jumper their Fosbury flop arch needs to be more pronounced is knowledge of performance).

practice_questions.text: State two sources of extrinsic feedback available to a performer in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct sources from: a coach or teacher giving verbal instructions; a teammate's comments; video analysis or video replay; heart rate monitor or performance data; scoreboard or result display; crowd reaction. Both answers must be qualitatively different sources to earn 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how knowledge of results and knowledge of performance each help an athlete improve. Use a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining knowledge of results: information about the outcome (score, time, distance) that tells the performer whether they succeeded or not, providing motivation. 1 mark for explaining knowledge of performance: information about the quality of the movement or technique used, pointing to what specifically needs to change. 1 mark for a relevant sporting example illustrating either or both (e.g. a swimmer learning their race time is 0.4 seconds slower than their personal best is KR; being told their tumble-turn is losing them 0.3 seconds is KP).

practice_questions.text: Explain why positive feedback is particularly important for beginner performers in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining positive feedback as information that tells the performer what they did correctly. 1 mark for explaining that it reinforces the correct movement pattern in memory, making repetition more likely. 1 mark for linking to the beginner context: beginners make frequent errors and their confidence and motivation can be fragile, so reinforcing what is right encourages continued participation. 1 mark for a specific sporting example or further development (e.g. a beginner basketball player is told 'your shooting stance is perfect' — this confirms a technique she should repeat and helps her build a reliable kinaesthetic reference point).

practice_questions.text: A junior badminton coach works with two groups: a Year 7 beginners' class learning the overhead clear for the first time, and a county under-16 squad preparing for a regional tournament. Evaluate how the coach should differ in the type and focus of feedback given to each group, and which approach is more likely to produce lasting improvement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): identifies and explains at least two contrasting feedback strategies for each group, linking each strategy to a specific reason grounded in the developmental difference between beginners and experienced performers. For beginners: positive feedback to build confidence; extrinsic feedback because intrinsic awareness is unreliable; knowledge of results as it is simple to understand; overloading with KP can confuse and demotivate. For the county squad: knowledge of performance to address fine technical detail; negative feedback welcomed at this level; well-developed intrinsic feedback can be trusted to supplement coaching. Reaches a balanced, reasoned conclusion about which approach produces more lasting improvement (e.g. KP + trusted intrinsic = deeper learning for elite, but positive/extrinsic = greater long-term retention for beginners if it keeps them engaged). Sustained sporting application throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies appropriate feedback for each group with explanation; at least one named feedback type per group; sporting context present but may be brief; conclusion present.

Developing (2 marks): makes relevant points about beginners needing simpler or more encouraging feedback; development limited; sporting application minimal or absent; one-sided argument.

Emerging (1 mark): basic points only (e.g. 'give more positive feedback to beginners'); no sporting application; no balance.

practice_questions.text:
Which fitness test is used to measure cardiovascular endurance?
A) Illinois agility test
B) Stork stand test
C) Cooper 12-minute run
D) Sit and reach test
practice_questions.marks: C — Cooper 12-minute run. [1 mark] (Also accept: multi-stage fitness test, if both options were listed.)

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'agility'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying agility as the ability to change body position quickly; 1 mark for specifying accurately while moving (accept: with speed and control; quickly and accurately).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows vertical jump scores for four athletes before and after a 10-week plyometric training programme.

Athlete | Score before (cm) | Score after (cm)
Dan     | 38                | 45
Ellie   | 41                | 50
Fatima  | 36                | 43
George  | 44                | 52

Calculate the mean improvement in vertical jump score across all four athletes. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly calculating each individual improvement (Dan: 7; Ellie: 9; Fatima: 7; George: 8); 1 mark for summing correctly (7 + 9 + 7 + 8 = 31) and dividing by 4; 1 mark for the correct final answer: 7.75 cm (accept 7.8 or 8 cm). Units required (cm) for the final answer mark.

practice_questions.text:
A county-level badminton player wants to know which fitness tests are most relevant for measuring her sport-specific fitness. Interpret the data below and suggest which test results are most meaningful for her performance.

Test              | Result
Cooper run        | 2,450 m
Illinois agility  | 16.4 seconds
Vertical jump     | 42 cm
Ruler drop        | 18 cm

Explain which two results are most important for her and why.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the Illinois agility test result (16.4 seconds) as most relevant, with a reason (badminton requires frequent direction changes to reach the shuttlecock across the court — agility is central to performance); 1 mark for identifying the ruler drop / reaction time (18 cm) as the second most important, with a reason (fast reaction time allows the player to respond to smashes and drops from the opponent before they can place the shuttlecock beyond her reach); 1 mark for quoting the specific figures from the table in the explanation; 1 mark for a valid evaluation of the other results (e.g. Cooper run is less critical than in endurance sports because rallies are short bursts; vertical jump is useful but not the primary performance-limiting factor in badminton).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a gymnast competing on the balance beam requires balance and flexibility as two of their most important fitness components.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining balance (the ability to retain the centre of mass over its base of support): the gymnast must maintain balance on a 10 cm-wide beam throughout their routine; 1 mark for applying balance to a named movement (e.g. holding a scale on one leg requires static balance); 1 mark for explaining flexibility (the range of movement possible at a joint): extreme joint mobility is needed to perform splits, walkovers and leaps to the required technical standard; 1 mark for applying flexibility to a named movement (e.g. a backbend walkover demands extreme spinal and hip flexibility to complete safely and score high artistic marks).

practice_questions.text: A PE teacher is designing a fitness testing programme for a Year-11 athletics squad. The squad includes 100 m sprinters and 1500 m runners. Evaluate which fitness components and tests are most important for each group, and whether any components are equally important for both.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Full range of components covered for both event groups, each with precise definitions and named OCR tests. 100 m: reaction time (ruler drop — leaving the blocks immediately); power (vertical jump — explosive acceleration from blocks); speed (30 m sprint — maximum velocity during the race); muscular endurance (sustaining maximal effort for 10-12 seconds). 1500 m: cardiovascular endurance (Cooper run / multi-stage — sustained oxygen supply over 4+ minutes); muscular endurance (press-up/sit-up — repeated muscle contractions over several laps); speed (30 m sprint — finishing kick); flexibility (sit and reach — stride efficiency and injury prevention). Shared components: muscular endurance (both events require it, though for different durations and intensities); speed (both benefit from speed, though it is the primary goal only for sprinters). Evaluation addresses trade-offs: sprint testing (reaction time, power) would be irrelevant data for a distance runner's training programme; cardiovascular endurance testing is largely irrelevant for a 100 m sprinter. Justified conclusion about how component priorities differ by event and why the teacher should test selectively. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): Most components covered for both groups with accurate definitions; named tests included; comparison made; conclusion reached; some minor gaps.

Developing (2 marks): Components identified for one or both groups; limited test knowledge; some sporting application; one-sided or lacking comparison.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one or two components with minimal explanation; little or no reference to tests or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify which letter of the SPOR acronym represents the idea that fitness gains can be lost when training stops.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: R — Reversibility.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'progressive overload' as it applies to a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the training load must be increased; 1 mark for stating that this increase must be gradual (over time) so the body continues to adapt and improve (accept: the stimulus must increase because the body adapts to the current load and no longer improves without a new challenge).

practice_questions.text: Describe how the FITT principles can be applied to help a club-level tennis player improve their cardiovascular endurance during pre-season.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for applying any three of the four FITT variables to the scenario with specific detail. Frequency example: train 4 times a week rather than twice, as cardiovascular gains require more sessions (1). Intensity example: set sessions at 70–80% of maximum heart rate to work in the aerobic training zone (1). Time example: sessions of 45–60 minutes to ensure sustained aerobic demand (1). Type example: use continuous training (e.g. cycling, running) to develop cardiovascular endurance specifically (1). Each answer must include the variable name and a specific application.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a coach can use the principle of specificity when designing a training programme for a 400 m track cyclist.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining specificity (training must match the demands of the sport/activity); 1 mark for explaining the specific energy system demands of 400 m track cycling (high-intensity anaerobic effort over approximately 40–50 seconds, with significant lactic acid production); 1 mark for explaining how training type should reflect this (interval training or HIIT on the bike, not long-distance continuous running); 1 mark for explaining how muscle specificity applies (training the quadriceps, gluteals and hip flexors through cycling-specific movements rather than gym exercises that do not replicate the cycling action).

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level distance runner has been following the same 10 km running programme for three months with no improvement in race times. Analyse how the SPOR and FITT principles could be used to redesign the programme so that it leads to further performance improvements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): identifies that the lack of improvement is explained by the principles of overload and progression — the body has adapted to the current stimulus; applies at least three FITT variables specifically (e.g. increase frequency from 3 to 5 sessions per week; increase intensity by introducing 80–85% max HR threshold runs; increase time of long runs by 10% per week); identifies specificity as supporting continued running-based sessions; raises reversibility to advise against abrupt rest periods; addresses recovery by recommending planned rest days; provides a coherent analysis of how these changes would lead to further cardiovascular and muscular endurance adaptation. Sporting context maintained throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): identifies progressive overload as the issue; applies two or more FITT variables with some specificity; some reference to sporting context.

Developing (2 marks): identifies that training needs to be harder or more varied; limited use of SPOR/FITT terminology.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant principle mentioned with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A school sports coach is designing an annual training programme for a Year 11 football squad. Evaluate how effectively the SPOR principles can be applied to team sport training compared to individual sport training, considering both the benefits and the challenges for a football coach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): evaluates each principle of training with a two-sided argument. Specificity: in individual sports (e.g. marathon running) specificity is straightforward — one performer, one event; in football, specificity is harder because different positions require different fitness profiles (a goalkeeper needs different components from a midfielder), so a whole-squad programme may not be fully specific for every player. Overload and progression: easy to apply individually; harder in team training because players start from different fitness baselines — a blanket 10% increase in session intensity may overload some players while under-loading others. Reversibility: applies equally to both; coaches of both individual and team sport must plan for off-season maintenance. Rest and recovery: in team sport, fixture schedules may not allow ideal recovery between matches, requiring careful management of training load in-season. Evaluates the overall effectiveness, naming specific football examples and contrasting with individual sport examples throughout. Balanced argument sustained.

Secure (3–4 marks): all four principles covered with some two-sided argument; mostly applied to football with some comparison to individual sport; generally accurate.

Developing (2 marks): at least two principles covered; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1 mark): basic reference to one or two principles with minimal analysis.

before.exam_tip_html: On a “6-mark Evaluate” question about training principles or a training programme, the most common error is writing a one-sided answer: listing only benefits or only limitations. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. Structure your answer: state the principle and its benefit for performance, then consider a limitation or a sport where the principle is harder to apply, and link each point to a named sporting example. For shorter “define” or “describe” questions, precision matters: “progression” must include the idea that the training load is gradually increased over time, not just that you train harder — one-word answers lose the second mark. Also check: OCR names four principles — Specificity, Progression, Overload and Reversibility — and there is no Tedium principle. Confusing this with other boards’ acronyms is a common error.

practice_questions.text: Identify one emotional benefit of regular participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: improved self-esteem or confidence; better stress management; more positive body image. Accept precise or descriptive answers.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'wellbeing'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition: a positive state across physical, emotional and social dimensions / feeling satisfied and capable. 1 mark for development: includes both the absence of illness and the presence of positive functioning across all three health dimensions; or gives an example distinguishing wellbeing from mere fitness (e.g. a person can be physically fit yet have poor emotional wellbeing if they suffer from anxiety or low self-esteem).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows participation rates and self-reported wellbeing scores for three groups of adults at a local sports centre.

Group | Weeks of exercise per year | Mean wellbeing score (out of 10)
A (0–5 weeks) | 3 weeks | 4.7
B (20–30 weeks) | 25 weeks | 6.9
C (40+ weeks) | 48 weeks | 8.2

Calculate the difference in mean wellbeing score between Group A and Group C, and suggest what this tells us about the relationship between exercise and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: 8.2 - 4.7 = 3.5 points (accept 3.5). 1 mark for showing working and stating the unit (points on the wellbeing scale). 1 mark for a valid inference: the 3.5-point difference in wellbeing scores suggests that higher levels of regular exercise are associated with substantially greater wellbeing, indicating a positive relationship between frequency of participation and wellbeing.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows the bone density measurements (g/cm²) of two groups of 65-year-old women: those who have exercised regularly for 20 years and those who have not.

Group | Mean bone density (g/cm²)
Active (regular exercise) | 1.08
Inactive (little or no exercise) | 0.79

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of regular exercise on bone density in older women.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that active women have higher mean bone density than inactive women (1.08 vs 0.79 g/cm²). 1 mark for quoting both figures to support the comparison. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone remodelling, maintaining or increasing density over time. 1 mark for the health implication: the 0.29 g/cm² difference suggests regular exercise significantly reduces the risk of osteoporosis and fractures in older adults.

practice_questions.text: Explain how regular participation in team sport can improve both emotional and social wellbeing for a 14-year-old.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an emotional benefit (improved self-esteem/confidence). 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (achieving a goal or developing a skill in team sport builds self-efficacy; exercise releases serotonin, reducing stress and anxiety). 1 mark for identifying a social benefit (making friends; sense of belonging to a group). 1 mark for linking to the 14-year-old context (adolescence is a period when peer relationships and self-image are especially important; team sport provides structured social contact that reduces loneliness and builds communication skills).

practice_questions.text: A health promotion officer argues that regular physical activity is the single most important factor in improving the wellbeing of older adults aged 65 and over. Evaluate this claim, considering physical, emotional and social wellbeing benefits.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): presents a balanced, sustained evaluation with points across all three wellbeing dimensions applied specifically to older adults; argues the case for physical activity (CHD prevention, bone density maintenance, reduced Type 2 diabetes risk, stress reduction, reduced loneliness through group exercise); presents a counter-argument with development (diet, social support networks, healthcare access also contribute to wellbeing; not all older adults can participate in exercise due to disability or chronic illness; some emotional wellbeing issues require professional intervention beyond exercise); reaches a justified conclusion about whether physical activity is the single most important factor. Sporting examples for this age group (walking groups, yoga, bowls, swimming) anchored throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): all three dimensions covered; case for physical activity and at least one counter-argument; sporting context mostly present; conclusion present.

Developing (2 marks): physical and one other dimension; some points about physical activity benefits; limited balance or counter-argument; conclusion may be present but not fully justified.

Emerging (1 mark): basic points about exercise being good for health; one-dimensional; no evaluation of relative importance.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes HIIT?
A) Sustained exercise at a constant pace for at least 20 minutes
B) Short bursts of near-maximal effort alternated with brief rest periods
C) Moving around a series of exercise stations with different fitness aims
D) Explosive bounding movements to develop muscular power
practice_questions.marks: B) Short bursts of near-maximal effort alternated with brief rest periods [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of circuit training compared to continuous training.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two distinct advantages, for example: It can target multiple components of fitness in one session (1); it can be adapted by changing stations, rest periods or resistance (1); it can replicate sport-specific movements (1); it provides variety, which supports motivation (1). Responses must be qualitatively different to earn both marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how plyometric training develops muscular power.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the muscle undergoes a rapid lengthening phase first (1); elastic energy is stored in the muscle and tendon during this phase (1); this is immediately followed by a powerful shortening contraction (1); the rapid transition between phases (the stretch-shortening cycle) produces a greater power output than a concentric contraction alone (1). Any three of the above, clearly described.

practice_questions.text: Explain why fartlek training is more appropriate for a football player than continuous training.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: fartlek varies speed and intensity throughout the session, including bursts of high-intensity effort (1); this mirrors the intermittent demands of football, where players alternate between jogging, sprinting and walking (1); continuous training maintains a steady pace and develops aerobic endurance only (1); football requires both aerobic and anaerobic capacity, and fartlek training stresses both energy systems (1). Full marks require both an explanation of what fartlek does AND why this is more appropriate for football than continuous training.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level long jumper wants to increase her explosive leg power over a 12-week training block. Analyse the use of plyometric training and weight training as methods she could use to achieve this goal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of both methods. Identifies advantages of plyometrics (replicates the stretch-shortening cycle of the take-off, develops power quickly, sport-specific) and limitations (high injury risk if technique is poor, requires strength base). Identifies advantages of weight training (builds the muscular strength base that underpins power; load and rep ranges can be adjusted; low injury risk with correct technique) and limitations (less sport-specific than plyometrics; muscular hypertrophy may not directly translate to explosive power). Applies both methods specifically to long jump demands. May recommend a combination. Uses accurate terminology throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): discusses both methods with some application to long jump; advantages and limitations present for at least one method; generally accurate.

Developing (2 marks): relevant points about one method; limited sporting application.

Emerging (1 mark): names one method with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A sprint coach is designing an interval training session for a 100 m sprinter. Explain how the work:rest ratio should be set to ensure the anaerobic energy system is targeted, and why this is important for the sprinter's performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: the work period should be short and at maximal intensity (above 80% max HR / all-out sprint) (1); the rest period should be longer than the work period to allow anaerobic energy stores to partially recover (1); for example, a 10-second maximal sprint followed by 50–60 seconds of rest would target the anaerobic system (1); this is important because a 100 m sprint is entirely anaerobic — the race lasts under 12 seconds and the intensity is too high for aerobic respiration to meet the energy demand (1).

practice_questions.text: Identify one physical consequence of living a sedentary lifestyle.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: obesity; coronary heart disease (CHD); hypertension (high blood pressure); Type 2 diabetes. Accept a brief explanation if the term alone is not used.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sedentary lifestyle'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the basic definition: a way of living characterised by very little physical activity / spending most of the day sitting or inactive. 1 mark for development: a specific example of sedentary behaviour (e.g. spending most waking hours at a screen or desk without structured exercise) or a named consequence (e.g. increasing the risk of obesity and coronary heart disease).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows data about a sample of 200 adults over five years.

Activity level | Developed Type 2 diabetes | Did not develop Type 2 diabetes
Active (150+ min/week) | 8 | 92
Sedentary (under 30 min/week) | 41 | 59

Using the data, calculate the percentage of sedentary adults in the sample who developed Type 2 diabetes, and explain what this suggests about the link between inactivity and diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: 41 out of 100 sedentary adults = 41%. 1 mark for stating the answer with the unit: 41%. 1 mark for a valid inference: 41% of sedentary adults developed Type 2 diabetes compared to only 8% of active adults, suggesting a strong association between physical inactivity and the development of Type 2 diabetes, likely because inactivity reduces insulin sensitivity.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows the mean resting blood pressure and BMI of adults in two groups: those who exercise at least three times per week and those who are sedentary.

Group | Mean resting systolic BP (mmHg) | Mean BMI
Regularly active | 118 | 24.3
Sedentary | 139 | 31.7

Interpret what the data shows about the relationship between sedentary behaviour, BMI and blood pressure.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that sedentary adults have a higher mean BMI (31.7 vs 24.3) and higher mean blood pressure (139 vs 118 mmHg). 1 mark for quoting both pairs of figures. 1 mark for explaining the link: a BMI over 30 indicates obesity; excess body fat contributes to arterial narrowing and loss of vessel elasticity, raising resting blood pressure. 1 mark for the health implication: the 21 mmHg difference in blood pressure suggests sedentary adults in this sample are at significantly greater risk of hypertension, stroke and CHD.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a sedentary lifestyle can lead to both low self-esteem and loneliness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining the link between inactivity and low self-esteem: inactivity can lead to weight gain and a negative body image, reducing confidence in physical settings. 1 mark for developing this point: reduced confidence leads to withdrawal from sport and social activity, creating a cycle where low self-esteem reinforces further inactivity. 1 mark for explaining the link between inactivity and loneliness: physical activity is a major vehicle for social interaction; without it, opportunities for social contact are reduced. 1 mark for developing this point: sustained social withdrawal leads to loneliness, which itself has negative health consequences (higher blood pressure, poorer mental health), potentially compounding the other consequences of the sedentary lifestyle.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the short-term and long-term consequences of a sedentary lifestyle on a person's physical and emotional health.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): analyses at least two physical consequences (e.g. obesity, CHD, hypertension, Type 2 diabetes) with clear mechanisms and a sustained analytical chain connecting them; analyses at least one emotional consequence (low self-esteem) with its mechanism; distinguishes between shorter-term onset (low self-esteem from inactivity developing relatively quickly) and longer-term disease risk (CHD, Type 2 diabetes developing over years); uses sporting or health context throughout; writes in developed prose rather than bullet points.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies physical and emotional consequences with some explanation of mechanism; at least two named conditions; some development and context present.

Developing (2 marks): names two or more consequences but mainly descriptive; limited or no mechanism; limited context.

Emerging (1 mark): one consequence named with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Identify the macronutrient that the body uses as its main and preferred energy source for all types of exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: carbohydrate (accept carbs, glucose or glycogen if clearly referring to the macronutrient).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'balanced diet'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the basic definition: a diet containing the correct proportions of all the nutrients the body needs. 1 mark for development: states the seven components (carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water); or states the approximate proportions (55-60% carbohydrate, 25-30% fat, 15-20% protein); or gives a sporting example (e.g. an endurance runner needs a higher carbohydrate proportion than a sedentary individual to fuel long training runs).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the daily macronutrient breakdown of two club-level swimmers during a training week.

Swimmer | Total daily energy | % from carbohydrate | % from protein | % from fat
Aisha | 2,800 kcal | 57% | 18% | 25%
Ben | 2,800 kcal | 44% | 22% | 34%

Using the data, identify which swimmer has a macronutrient balance within the recommended ranges for a balanced diet, and calculate the amount of energy Ben obtains from fat each day.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying Aisha as within balanced-diet ranges: carbohydrate 57% (within 55-60%), protein 18% (within 15-20%), fat 25% (within 25-30%). Ben is outside range (44% carbohydrate is below 55% minimum; 34% fat exceeds 30% maximum). 1 mark for correct calculation: 2,800 x 0.34 = 952 kcal from fat. 1 mark for stating the unit (kcal) and confirming Ben's fat intake exceeds the recommended maximum of 30%.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows heart rate data for two players during the final 20 minutes of a 90-minute football match played in hot conditions. Player A drank water at half-time; Player B drank nothing during the match.

Time | Player A heart rate (bpm) | Player B heart rate (bpm)
70 min | 148 | 163
80 min | 151 | 172
90 min | 149 | 181

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of dehydration on Player B's heart rate, and explain why this change occurred.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Player B's heart rate is consistently higher than Player A's across all three time points (163 vs 148 at 70 min, rising to 181 vs 149 at 90 min). 1 mark for quoting specific figures to support the comparison. 1 mark for linking the rising heart rate to dehydration increasing blood viscosity (thicker blood). 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: the heart must beat faster to maintain adequate blood flow to working muscles when blood is thicker, accelerating fatigue and performance decline in the final stages of the match.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an adequate intake of carbohydrate and protein would help a county-level rower prepare for and recover from a five-day intensive training camp.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining carbohydrate's role in preparation: stored as glycogen in muscles and liver, used as the primary fuel during high-intensity rowing training; adequate carbohydrate ensures glycogen stores are full before each session. 1 mark for explaining carbohydrate's role during the camp: replenishing glycogen stores after each session maintains energy availability for subsequent sessions across the five days. 1 mark for explaining protein's role in recovery: muscle fibres are broken down during intense rowing training; protein provides the amino acids needed for repair and adaptation (hypertrophy). 1 mark for a link to performance: insufficient protein slows repair, leaving the rower fatigued and limiting the training adaptations the camp is designed to produce.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level long-distance runner is preparing for her first half-marathon. Her coach has recommended she follow a carefully planned diet for the six weeks before the race. Evaluate the extent to which carbohydrate, protein and hydration are each important to her preparation and race performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): presents a balanced evaluation of all three nutritional factors applied specifically to a long-distance runner preparing for a half-marathon; argues the case for carbohydrate (primary fuel, glycogen loading in final days, sustained energy during the 90+ minute race); argues the case for protein (muscle repair across the six-week training block, limiting injury and supporting adaptation); argues the case for hydration (dehydration raises heart rate and blood viscosity, slows reactions, causes muscle cramps, particularly dangerous in a long-duration event); evaluates relative importance with justification (e.g. carbohydrate is arguably most critical on race day because glycogen depletion is the primary cause of 'hitting the wall'; however, without adequate protein across the training block there would be insufficient muscle adaptation to compete); at least one developed counter-argument; sporting application sustained throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): covers all three factors with explanation; links to the long-distance running context mostly present; some evaluation of relative importance; conclusion present.

Developing (2 marks): covers two factors accurately; links to the athlete context limited; limited evaluation; conclusion may be present but not fully justified.

Emerging (1 mark): one or two basic accurate points about nutrition or hydration with little sporting application or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify the fourth component of an OCR warm-up, which involves sport-specific exercises at increasing intensity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: dynamic movements.

practice_questions.text: State two physical benefits of completing a warm-up before exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two distinct physical benefits, for example: increased body temperature makes muscles more pliable, reducing the risk of strains (1); increased range of movement at joints as synovial fluid becomes less viscous (1); increased heart rate and cardiac output gradually prepare the cardiovascular system (1); increased oxygen delivery to working muscles (1); improved speed of muscle contraction as nerve impulses travel faster (1); improved pliability of ligaments and tendons (1). Two answers must be physiologically distinct to earn both marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how cooling down helps the body recover from intense exercise. Include reference to lactic acid in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: gradual reduction in intensity maintains elevated heart rate and blood flow to the muscles (1); sustained blood flow transports lactic acid away from the muscles to the liver for processing and removal (1); this reduces muscle acidity and helps prevent or minimise post-exercise stiffness (1); static stretching during the cool-down helps maintain muscle flexibility and reduce post-exercise tightness (1). Any three of the above, with lactic acid specifically referenced for at least one mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain why skill rehearsal is included as the final component of a warm-up, and how it differs from the pulse raiser.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: skill rehearsal involves sport-specific drills and movements practised at moderate intensity (1); it prepares the neuromuscular system by rehearsing the precise movement patterns required in the activity (1); it builds confidence and bridges the gap between general physical preparation and full competition demands (1); the pulse raiser is non-specific (general aerobic activity such as jogging) and focuses on raising heart rate and body temperature rather than rehearsing skills (1). Full marks require both an explanation of skill rehearsal's purpose AND a clear distinction from the pulse raiser.

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 county-level rugby team has 25 minutes before a regional semi-final. Their coach is planning a structured warm-up. Analyse the importance of each component of an effective warm-up for the rugby players before this match.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): all five components identified and each clearly linked to a physiological benefit specific to rugby. Pulse raiser: raises body temperature, increases heart rate and blood flow to muscles needed for explosive sprinting and tackling; mobility: loosens joints, particularly the hips, shoulders and neck which are under significant contact pressure in rugby; stretching: increases flexibility of hamstrings and hip flexors needed for sprinting, and shoulders for tackling and lifting; dynamic movements: includes sprint-and-change-of-direction drills replicating the demands of ruck and maul play; skill rehearsal: includes passing, lineout lifting and scrummaging technique rehearsal to prime neuromuscular pathways specific to rugby decision-making. Uses accurate physiological terminology throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): at least three components described with correct benefits; at least two benefits applied to rugby specifically; generally accurate terminology.

Developing (2 marks): two components identified and described; limited sporting application; one or more physiological effects correctly stated.

Emerging (1 mark): names one component or states one general benefit of warming up without development or application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of including both a warm-up and a cool-down in a training programme for a competitive swimmer who trains six days per week.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): evaluates both warm-up and cool-down with a balanced two-sided argument. Warm-up arguments for: raises body temperature (improves muscle pliability and speed of contraction needed for powerful stroke technique); increases blood flow and oxygen to muscles (supports aerobic energy system from the start of a session); mobilises shoulder and hip joints (high importance in swimming); skill rehearsal of stroke technique primes neuromuscular pathways. Warm-up arguments against/limitation: a swimmer training six days per week may find warm-up time cuts into overall session volume; time pressure in competition warm-up lanes. Cool-down arguments for: removes lactic acid accumulated during intense sprint sets; static stretching maintains shoulder flexibility (high relevance given overuse risk in swimmers); reduces muscle soreness, allowing quality training on consecutive days. Cool-down arguments against/limitation: swimmer fatigue and time pressure may reduce compliance; cool-down in cold pool water may be less effective than on land. Reaches a justified conclusion about relative importance, applying to swimming context throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): both warm-up and cool-down covered with some two-sided argument; mostly applied to swimming; generally accurate physiological content.

Developing (2 marks): one of warm-up or cool-down covered in more depth; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1 mark): basic statements about one component; little application to swimming; descriptive rather than evaluative.

before.exam_tip_html: On a “6-mark Evaluate” question about warm-up or cool-down, avoid simply listing components. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. For example, rather than writing “the pulse raiser raises heart rate,” develop it: “the pulse raiser gradually raises body temperature, which increases muscle pliability and reduces the risk of muscle strains — particularly important for a gymnast whose movements demand maximum hip and shoulder flexibility from the first routine.” For 2-mark “State Two” questions, ensure your two benefits are genuinely different physiological effects — “raises heart rate” and “increases blood flow” are related but distinct enough to earn two marks, whereas “raises heart rate” and “heart rate goes up” will only earn one. Note: OCR names five warm-up components, not four — mobility and dynamic movements are separate stages.

practice_questions.text: Identify one potential hazard specific to a fitness centre setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: free weights left on the floor as a trip hazard; incorrect weight machine settings trapping a limb; wet floor near a water fountain; absence of a spotter during heavy lifts; cables or resistance bands positioned at head height. Accept any specific, plausible fitness-centre hazard.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'personal protective equipment' (PPE) and give one example of its use in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a definition that identifies PPE as equipment worn to protect the body from impact or injury during sport; 1 mark for a correct sporting example (e.g. shin pads in football, a batting helmet in cricket, a mouthguard in rugby, a cycle helmet, knee pads in volleyball). Definition and example must both be present for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe two hazards that could cause injury on a playing field, and explain how each hazard could be managed.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for each of two distinct playing-field hazards (e.g. uneven ground causing ankle sprains; debris such as stones or glass causing cuts or trips; unanchored goalposts causing crush injuries if they fall; waterlogged or frozen ground increasing fall risk) and 1 mark for a correct corresponding management strategy (e.g. pre-match pitch inspection; removing debris before play; checking goalpost anchoring; postponing play in extreme weather). Award 1 mark for a correct hazard with no management strategy if only one hazard is described with its management. Do not award both marks for two versions of the same hazard (e.g. wet grass and slippery pitch).

practice_questions.text: Explain how using a warm-up and cool-down before and after exercise can help prevent injury.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: warm-up raises muscle temperature, making muscles more pliable and reducing the risk of strains during explosive movements (1); warm-up increases the pliability of tendons and ligaments, which are more elastic at higher temperatures (1); cool-down maintains blood flow to remove lactic acid and reduce post-exercise muscle stiffness, reducing the risk of injury in subsequent sessions (1); cool-down stretching helps muscles return to their resting length, reducing tightness that could cause compensatory movement patterns and injury in the next session (1).

practice_questions.text: A secondary school PE department is conducting a risk assessment for a swimming gala to be held in the school pool. Analyse the potential hazards present in this setting and how they could be minimised.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): identifies multiple swimming pool hazards with their injury mechanisms and corresponding management strategies, and analyses why each matters in the context of a school event. Slippery pool surrounds: risk of falls onto hard, non-absorbent surface causing head or limb fractures; managed by ensuring non-slip matting around the pool edge and enforcing a no-running rule. Diving into shallow water: risk of cervical spine fractures and serious head injury; managed by enforcing feet-first entry in shallow areas and clearly marking water depth. Overcrowding: risk of collisions during swimming; managed by using lane ropes and staggered heats. Inadequate supervision: a school gala has many young swimmers; managed by having qualified lifeguards positioned at opposite ends of the pool. Chemical hazards: pool chemicals (chlorine, pH adjustment) are hazardous; managed by ensuring storage areas are locked and only accessible to qualified staff. Demonstrates understanding of the link between hazard, injury mechanism and prevention throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): three or more hazards identified with correct injury mechanisms and management strategies; some analysis of why the measures matter in a school context.

Developing (2 marks): two hazards identified correctly; limited analysis; some management strategies.

Emerging (1 mark): one hazard named with minimal development or management strategy.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of personal protective equipment (PPE) and correct clothing and footwear as methods of preventing injury in sport, considering both their benefits and their limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): provides a balanced evaluation of both PPE and clothing/footwear, with benefits and limitations of each applied to named sporting examples. PPE benefits: absorbs or deflects impact forces that would otherwise cause fractures, lacerations or concussions (e.g. a rugby scrum cap reduces the severity of head impacts; shin pads protect the tibia in football). PPE limitations: can only protect the body part it covers; may limit range of movement or create a false sense of security leading to reckless play; must be correctly fitted to be effective — poorly fitting helmets may actually increase injury risk. Clothing/footwear benefits: sport-specific footwear provides appropriate grip and support (e.g. football boots on grass, swimming goggles protecting eyes from chlorine); compression garments support muscles and reduce strain risk. Clothing/footwear limitations: incorrect footwear in one setting may cause injury in another (e.g. metal studs on artificial turf); clothing cannot prevent all impact injuries and may not be a complete substitute for PPE in contact sports. Concludes with a justified assessment of which is more broadly effective or whether both are necessary. Sporting examples used throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): both strategies covered with some two-sided argument; sporting application present; generally accurate.

Developing (2 marks): at least one strategy covered with some benefit and limitation; limited balance; some sporting context.

Emerging (1 mark): basic statements about PPE or clothing; minimal sporting application; descriptive rather than evaluative.

before.exam_tip_html: On a “6-mark Evaluate” question about injury prevention, the mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument, and (c) sporting application. A common error is listing prevention strategies without explaining how they reduce injury — always link the strategy to the injury mechanism it prevents. For example: “Wearing shin pads in football reduces the risk of tibial fractures and lacerations from direct contact, because the pad absorbs and disperses the impact energy across a larger surface area.” For “Describe” questions about hazards, name the setting, name the specific hazard, and explain why it causes injury. Vague answers such as “the floor could be wet” without naming the setting or injury type will only earn one mark of a possible two or three. For that 6-mark question, weigh up which strategies are most effective and in which settings — PPE may be critical in contact sport but less relevant in swimming.
